summary.text: Changes in the Sun's output have been a main driver of Earth's climate change over the millions to billions of years of geologic time.
Satellites measuring the Sun since 1978 show its total output rising and falling by about 0.1% over the roughly 11-year solar cycle, with a stable average.
Those spacecraft observations show that recent global warming is not caused by changes in the Sun, and human-caused forcings are needed to reproduce late-20th-century warming.

facts.label: Early Sun
facts.value: 70% of today's power, 3–4 billion years ago

facts.label: Pre-1970s estimates
facts.value: Tree rings, sunspot counts and isotopes like ¹⁰Be

items.prompt: Billions of years ago the Sun was much weaker, yet Earth already had liquid water. What is one proposed explanation?

options.label: Earth sat much closer to the Sun back then
The oceans were too salty to freeze at all
Heat from the Moon kept the seas from freezing
The air held far more greenhouse gases than now

items.explain: This is the faint young Sun paradox, and one hypothesized solution is an atmosphere with much higher greenhouse gas levels.

items.prompt: Over one roughly 11-year solar cycle, by about how much does the Sun's total output rise and fall?

options.label: About 0.1%
About 5%
About 20%
About 50%

items.explain: Satellite measurements show total solar irradiance varies by about ±0.1% over the solar cycle.

items.prompt: Sunspot peaks have shrunk cycle after cycle since the 1960s, while the planet has warmed. What does that pattern point to?

options.label: A brighter Sun is driving the warming
Recent warming is not caused by the Sun
Fewer sunspots make Earth warmer
Sunspots have no link to solar activity

items.explain: Solar activity has been declining since the 1960s, and spacecraft data show recent warming is not caused by changes in the Sun.

items.prompt: Observations show the lower atmosphere warming while the stratosphere above it cools. Which cause do models link to that pattern?

options.label: A gradual brightening of the Sun
A run of large volcanic eruptions
A build-up of greenhouse gases
A rise in incoming cosmic rays

items.explain: Models and observations show greenhouse gases warm the troposphere but cool the stratosphere.

items.prompt: Europe ran cold during a 70-year stretch when the Sun showed almost no sunspots. Does that settle that the quiet Sun caused the cold?

options.label: Yes, the timing proves the Sun was the cause
Yes, since sunspots are what heat the Earth
No, volcanoes are another proposed cause
No, Europe was warm during that time

items.explain: The Maunder minimum overlapped the Little Ice Age, but whether low solar activity caused the cooling is debated, and one paper blamed volcanism.

items.prompt: Suppose the Sun entered a new 90-year stretch of low activity. What would that likely do to today's global warming?

options.label: Cancel greenhouse warming completely
Cool things slightly, far too little to offset it
Trigger a new ice age within decades
Speed the warming up even further

items.explain: A 2010 paper estimated such a lull would cut global temperatures by about 0.3 °C, far from enough to offset greenhouse gas forcing.
